questions.q: What does PHP's serialize() function produce?
o: A JSON string of the object
A string representation of an object's type and property values in PHP's custom format
A base64-encoded copy of the object
questions.x: serialize() produces a text string that encodes the object's class name, property count, and each property's type, name, and value. The format uses single-letter type codes (O for object, s for string, i for integer, b for boolean) followed by the data.
questions.h: serialize() produces a text string, not binary. What information about the object does PHP need to reconstruct it later?

questions.q: What does the letter O at the start of a PHP serialized string indicate?
questions.x: PHP uses type prefixes: O = Object, a = array, s = string, i = integer, b = boolean, N = null. O:14:"CustomTemplate" means an Object whose class name is 14 characters long and is called CustomTemplate.
questions.h: PHP serialization uses single-letter type codes. What type of data structure does uppercase O represent?

questions.q: Why is passing user-controlled data to unserialize() dangerous?
o: unserialize() runs base64 decode which can cause buffer overflows
unserialize() can instantiate any class available in the codebase, potentially triggering magic methods with dangerous behavior
PHP objects cannot be trusted because they ignore type checking
unserialize() makes a network call that can be redirected
questions.x: unserialize() reconstructs any PHP object from the string. If a class in scope has a magic method like __destruct() or __wakeup() that does something dangerous (deletes a file, sends a request), calling unserialize() with the right string triggers that behavior automatically.
questions.h: Think about what unserialize() does step by step. It creates a PHP object. What runs automatically when a PHP object is created or destroyed?

questions.q: What PHP property access modifier makes a property appear as \x00*\x00propertyName in serialized form?
questions.x: Protected properties are serialized with a null byte, asterisk, null byte prefix before the name (\x00*\x00name). Private properties use the class name between null bytes. Public properties have no prefix.
questions.h: PHP encodes visibility in serialized strings using special character sequences. Which modifier is represented by the null-asterisk-null sequence?

questions.q: What is the safest alternative to PHP serialization for storing user session data?
o: JSON, which only reconstructs plain data structures and cannot instantiate classes or trigger magic methods
PHP's var_export() output evaluated with eval()
questions.x: JSON decodes into plain arrays and scalars, never into class instances. There are no magic methods to trigger and no gadget chains to exploit. It is also language-neutral, making it easier to validate and inspect.
questions.h: The danger of unserialize() is that it creates full PHP objects. What data format only creates arrays and primitive values, never class instances?
